paper_title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.

Introduction In ongoing commercial operations, daily decisions reshape both the evidence an agent later observes and the working capital it retains. When buyer lets shelves run empty, unserved walk-in demand goes unrecorded in sales logs (Huh & Rusmevichientong, 2009; Besbes & Muharremoglu, 2013); when an account delivery falls short, the customer reduces subsequent orders weeks after the original shortfall; and when emergency local purchases cover missing inventory, immediate service is preserved at the expense of cash needed for future stock. Assigning credit across weeks of delayed feedback has challenged AI since Minsky (1961), because the agent must interpret observations partly generated by its own prior choices and adjust behavior before the full cost materializes (Polanyi, 1966). Recent work has begun to measure sustained operation, adaptation, and learning from interaction (Silver & Sutton, 2025). Commercial and multi-day benchmarks expose planning, diagnostics, and coordinated business effects (Backlund & Petersson, 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Raghuvanshi et al., 2026), behavioral audits separate collecting evidence or stating diagnosis from acting on it (Zhang et al., 2026a; Deb & Krishnan, 2026; Li & Ho, 2026), and stateful-versusstateless evaluations separate gains from accumulated experience from starting competence (Asawa et al., 2026). Training methods likewise use interaction-generated future states and continuations from restored intermediate states to improve multi-turn agents (Ross & Bagnell, 2014; Zhang et al., 2025; Zhang & Yang, 2026; Li et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a). These developments motivate common question, what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses? Our working hypothesis is that useful experience preserves the link between decision, the state in which it was made, and its later consequences; making relationships in those records explicit can guide better choices, while practicing from recorded states can make those choices more consistent. Testing this Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences Figure 1. The SMB Bench environment, matched conditions, and deterministic state replay. (a) Across 90 mornings, the buyer queries SQL records and daily supplier quotes, places wholesale case orders, sets customer shortfall protection, and updates persistent notes. Decisions reshape later evidence and cash through hidden walk-in demand during stockouts, multi-week customer order reductions after shortfalls, and 2.5 emergency-cover cash drain. (b) Every business runs under three conditions with identical buyer-visible Day-0 observations (normal, customer-loss, and Day-21 supplier-shock quarters) and supports deterministic replay from any committed morning to compare alternative actions or continue archived runs. hypothesis requires measuring what an agent records, what it does next, and whether the response improves business profit, three achievements that prove separable throughout our study. To investigate all three in one system, we build SMB Bench (Bansal et al., 2026), calibrated 90-day perishable wholesale environment (Wang et al., 2025) (Figure 1; benchmark report and public trace dataset). Across six businesses and 18 tasks, each store runs under normal, customer-loss, and supplier-shock conditions with identical buyer-visible Day0 observations alongside non-LLM reference policies and deterministic morning replay (Section 2), letting us test whether behavior changes specifically when decisions carry delayed penalties and whether missed actions would have helped (Section 3). Across 859 scored runs of 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform Fixed Buying Rule (+$6,412 versus +$10,795 Scripted Expert). In the nine-model behavioral cohort, agents stocked below 60% of their own written forecasts in 78.7% (107 of 136) of audited cases; across quarters with reactive accounts, 21.4% contained written link between falling orders and prior shortfalls, and in 3.7% of reactive-account quarters the agent both recorded that link and extended protection to all accounts within three mornings of the note (Section 4). Using SMB Benchs replay on Qwen3.8-27B, we extract operational rules from training-business records, refine prompt and optimizer choices on validation business, and train on continuations from archived frontier mornings rather than copied transcripts (Section 5). On sealed test business, the final system finishes ahead of 8 of 16 leaderboard models ($4,495 versus +$1,969 for GPT-6 Astra); holding the unseen evaluation instructions fixed, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently, cutting protection reversals from 5.8 to 1.0 per quarter and quarters losing over $10,000 from 25% to 8% while measured recognition of stockout censoring changed little (84.7% to 85.6%) and the additional profit difference remained uncertain (+$1,489 $1,133 standard error). Consistently protecting customers in turn exposed an upstream coordination problem across inventory buffers, supplier lead times, and cash (Section 6), clarifying what autonomous experience-learning agents must coordinate next (Lin et al., 2026; Shalev et al., 2026). We introduce SMB Bench, calibrated 90-day wholesale environment pairing matched Day-0 normal and consequence conditions with non-LLM reference policies and deterministic replay from any morning. We release an 859-run frontier evaluation and trace dataset across 16 models, connecting controlled cover trajectories, written-forecast audits, and restock replays to separate recorded diagnosis from consistent operational action. We turn archived runs into reusable training experience for Qwen3.8-27B, testing what changes on sealed business under fixed evaluation instructions and di2 Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences agnosing the supply and cash limits that consistent customer protection exposes. 2. SMB Bench To study delayed consequences cleanly, an environment must couple daily choices across weeks while keeping every intermediate state reproducible. SMB Bench places one model on the produce buying desk of wholesaler over 90-day quarter (d = 0, . . . , 89). Each store sells 18 to 20 perishable items to walk-in shoppers at shelf or markdown prices and to six restaurant and catering accounts at locked order-day prices. Every morning opens at 5 a.m. as fresh conversation showing status dashboard, the buyer prompt, and the models persistent notebook (notes.md, up to 16 files and 32,000 bytes). With up to 60 tool calls per morning, the buyer queries DuckDB SQL tables (query_records, list_tables, describe_table), inspects daily supplier quotes (list_offers), places case orders (place_ purchase_order), sets per-item or wildcard (*) shortfall protection (set_shortfall_cover), and updates notes before calling advance_day alone. Fixed simulator rules run the rest of the day, receiving trucks before store open, filling account lines and automatic 6 a.m. local cover at 2.54 wholesale quotes, serving 16 hours of walk-in sales, stepping down walk-in prices past markdown age, discarding expired lots, and settling bills. Episodes are graded once after Day 89 on the net change in business value. Purchases remain inventory assets until sold or written off, so the graders accounting bridge decomposes that change as Profit = Vclose Vopen = Ccogs Cwaste Cshort Cops Clost, (1) where is walk-in and account revenue net of customer return refunds, Ccogs is the wholesale and 6 a.m. local purchase cost of sold units, Cwaste writes off expired, culled, and inspection-rejected lots plus closing stock that projected demand cannot sell before expiry, Cshort is the 5% compensation on first due-day shorted account value, and Cops covers dispatch, delivery, receiving, refusal, disposal, storage, interest, and overhead fees (0.1647 baseline revenue in overhead, putting the reference buyer near 3% net margin) and pending refund and claim reserves, net of supplier claim recoveries. Clost deducts the 28-day closing customerdemand reserve at 30% of price when prior shorts have shrunk account orders. Each unit bought therefore enters profit exactly once, through Ccogs when sold or Cwaste when lost, and the closing write-down and Clost block quarter-end gaming. Realism comes from public datasets checked against wholesaler workflows with industry partner GetASAP, using zero private company records. Hourly walk-in demand and stockout censoring patterns are fit from FreshRetailNet50K (Wang et al., 2025), price and freight spreads draw on USDA/ERS reports, and cooler groups (cold_dry, cold_humid, cool, warm) and physical lifetimes (7 to 240 days) follow UC Davis postharvest guides. Wholesaler consultations grounded two cross-product couplings, supplier minimum-weight thresholds for dispatch fees and shared working capital (spendable cash plus unused credit minus open payables and open purchase orders, tracked as available_to_commit), funding both wholesale orders and 6 a.m. local cover. Before freezing the benchmark, we screened 42 candidate tasks across 168 worlds so scores isolate delayed adaptation rather than Day-0 clues (Table 4 in Appendix B). Every world matched its twin control byte-for-byte on all buyervisible Day-0 surfaces and passed an independent accounting audit. Admission required 0.25% baseline-revenue damage to an ignoring buyer in at least 4 of 6 stores, feasible remedy, and 0/0/0 false positives on blind-habit, generous-default, and twin-chance checks. Four mechanisms fell below the 4-store materiality bar, leaving 18 tasks across six businesses, 6 normal quarters, 6 customer-loss quarters with reactive accounts (shortfalls shrink future account orders, costing two-thirds of volume after three weeks of 10% shorts), and 6 supplier-shock quarters (reactive accounts plus the cheapest suppliers late and cancel rates jump on orders placed from Day 21 onward). Every task is anchored by three non-LLM controllers. Each morning, the Fixed Buying Rule (+$6,412 mean across 18 tasks, +$10,051 normal, +$4,592 changed) reads the past 14 days of censoring-adjusted walk-in and account sales, booked account lines, on-hand and in-transit stock, and current supplier quotes; it orders enough from the cheapest quote to cover due account orders plus delivery lead time and 1.5-day buffer, covers shortfalls locally only within 5% of contract price, keeps no notes, and never alters its rule when conditions shift. The Scripted Expert Buyer (+$10,795) encodes wholesaler practices on buyer-visible data, consolidating supplier orders to save dispatch fees, covering all accounts from Day 0, and holding lead-time buffers. The Perfect-Foresight Solver (+$16,923) replans daily with oracle future knowledge. Paired with deterministic replay from any committed morning, these matched conditions and reference policies provide states and outcomes that can be reused for counterfactual testing and training. 3. Evaluation and Behavioral Measures To distinguish starting policies, generic mid-quarter drift, and responses to delayed consequences, our benchmark analysis combines full-leaderboard scoring with pre-specified trace audits and replay tests  (Table 1)  . All 16 models ran the unedited benchmark prompt across all 18 tasks (6 businesses 3 conditions, 3 repeats per cell), yielding 859 valid scored quarters of 864 attempted (five runs ended on 3 Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences provider execution errors and remain unscored, while 20 infrastructure-interrupted runs resumed deterministically from their last committed morning). Because store sizes span $91K to $340K in 90-day baseline sales potential, task comparisons report both dollar profit and baseline-revenuenormalized margin points over the Fixed Buying Rule in the identical world  (Table 5)  . Detailed behavioral analysis covers the nine models in the original benchmark release (485 scored runs across GPT6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Grok 4.7, GLM 5.3, and Muse Wonder 1.0), while leaderboard comparisons include all 16 evaluated models. Within that cohort, forecast execution audits every product-morning where model recorded an explicit numeric demand estimate in its notes (136 cases), comparing stocked quantity against its stated forecast. Counterfactual restock replays examine weeks with at least 25% out-of-stock hours where GPT-6 Astra (26 cases) or GPT-6.1 Sol (24 cases) wrote note calling for higher stock, replaying the episode with those noted orders placed. For delayed customer loss, we audit all 323 scored quarters with reactive accounts, which include both the customer-loss and supplier-shock tasks (9 models 12 tasks), alongside 162 normal-quarter controls of the same businesses. run records written attribution when notes or reasoning explicitly link falling account orders to the buyers prior delivery shortfalls, and prompt action when standing shortfall cover is extended to all six accounts within three mornings of that note. Cover rules already enabled during Day 01 initial setup are excluded from mid-quarter course changes. Finally, to test controlled adaptation over time, we track each models daily share of account-product lines protected by shortfall cover across Days 0 to 88 (stopping before Day 89, when newly set cover can no longer protect an order) and compare the Day-14-to-Day-88 rise in customer-loss quarters alone (6 tasks, 18 runs per model, excluding suppliershock quarters) against the same models normal quarters via 10,000-resample task-and-run bootstrap intervals. 4. Frontier Results Across all 16 frontier models and 859 scored runs, only three models finish ahead of the Fixed Buying Rule (+$6,412 per quarter) on average (Figure 2a), led by GPT-6 Astra (+$7,749), Gemini 4 Carbon (+$7,703), and Claude Fable 5.2 (+$7,275), down to GPT-6 Luna at $8,667. None beats the Fixed Buying Rule reliably in every run, and every model trails the Scripted Expert Buyer (+$10,795, 64% of the Solvers +$16,923) by more than $3,000 per quarter. Models often record relevant diagnosis without making the corresponding change in later purchases. Across the 485-run behavioral cohort, every model buys 5% to 42% less produce by weight than the Fixed Buying Rule, and runs that buy less earn less within every model as well as across models (ρ = +0.84, Figure 2b). Across 136 cases where model wrote down its own demand forecast, it stocked below 60% of that estimate in 107 cases (78.7%). After seven consecutive stockout days on broccoli, GPT-6 Astra recorded the shortage in its notes, continued ordering well below supplier offers, and stayed out of stock on nine of the next ten days. Broccoli has stocked out for seven consecutive days, so Ill test modest increase in its forecast while trimming tomorrows tomato, grape, carrot and potato orders. Following product-weeks out of stock at least 25% of store hours, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol added +0.09 and +0.07 days of stock, raising orders when their own notes called for restocking in 3 of 26 and 5 of 24 cases. Replaying those episodes with the noted orders placed increased quarterly net value by 1.3% to 2.7% of sales, confirming under the simulator that executing the recorded restock plan improved profit. Delayed customer loss shows the same gap between recorded diagnosis and timely action. Across 323 quarters with reactive accounts (customer-loss and supplier-shock tasks), models tied falling orders to their own shortfalls in writing in 69 runs (21.4%) and protected all six accounts within three days in 12 runs (3.7%, Figure 2c). Grok 4.7 recorded that connection in 26 runs and acted within three days in zero while exposed account orders fell past 80%; Claude Opus 5.5 attributed falling orders to external demand on Day 33 before enabling cover five weeks late on Day 71. Mid-quarter course changes were nine percentage points more frequent in quarters with reactive accounts than in normal quarters (20% versus 11%). Comparing daily shortfall protection in customer-loss quarters against each models own normal-quarter control separates three distinct patterns (Figure 3). First, by Day 14, Gemini 4 Argon has reached full cover and GPT-6 Astra already covers 93.5% of account products, leaving little room for further rise during the measured window; this comparison measures later adaptation and does not exclude learning before Day 14. Second, several models drift upward for reasons also present in calm quarters; Claude Fable 5.1 raises cover by +13.2 points in customer-loss quarters versus +25.6 in normal quarters (12.4 difference). Third, isolated runs respond directly to customer attrition without producing dependable model-wide shift. GPT-6.1 Sol rises +6.8 points more from Day 14 in customer-loss quarters than in normal quarters (95% interval 2.8 to +17.9), driven by two runs climbing from 9% to 79% and 10% to 59%, and across all nine models (mean difference +1.5 points; Table 6 in Appendix B) zero models achieve 95% interval strictly above zero over the Day 14 to Day 88 window. Remaining Coordination Failure Protecting customers consistently exposed an upstream requirement across ordering, supplier lead times, and cash. On Business 6, the trained policy received supply equivalent to 88.8% of total demand, close to GPT-6 Astras 88.6%, yet fulfilled less walk-in demand (74.1% versus 80.3%), spent $11,868 versus $4,190 per quarter on 6 a.m. emergency local purchases across 72 of 90 days, and trailed Astra by $6,465 (Figure 6a, top). Checking recorded supplier offers and morning purchasing constraints (available_ to_commit) across all 12 test quarters shows that cooler limits (0.0%), case caps (0.7%), and 3-day prepay terms (9.7%) rarely caused these local buys (Figure 6a, bottom). Stateful and Economic Agent Benchmarks Interactive coding, web, and tool benchmarks test multistep execution across bounded tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Kwa et al., 2025), while recent stateful benchmarks examine sustained commercial operation and adaptation (Backlund & Petersson, 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). StoreBench combines persistent commerce environment, replay, operational diagnostics, and post-training (Raghuvanshi et al., 2026); CEO-Bench studies delayed business effects across coordinated decisions (Chen et al., 2026); and Continual Learning Bench compares stateful against stateless runs to separate accumulated experience from starting competence (Asawa et al., 2026). Close behavioral studies likewise examine where diagnosis and action diverge, as STOCKTAKE compares stated diagnosis against subsequent control (Deb & Krishnan, 2026) and RetailBench tracks evidence acquisition, action conversion, and followup (Zhang et al., 2026a) alongside multi-stage inference audits (Li & Ho, 2026). Within this agenda (Minsky, 1961; Silver & Sutton, 2025), SMB Bench combines matched Day-0 consequence conditions, missed-action replays, and archived frontier mornings in one study where the buyers own decisions alter later sales evidence and cash. 7.2. Interactive Imitation and State-Continuation RL Off-policy imitation compounds errors under state drift (Ross et al., 2011), whereas branching from visited states under cost-to-go evaluation lets learners improve upon imperfect reference policies (AggreVaTe, Ross & Bagnell, 2014; LOLS, Chang et al., 2015; Go-Explore, Ecoffet et al., 2021; VinePPO, Kazemnejad et al., 2024). Recent agent-training methods build directly on interaction states and restored prefixes, using action-generated future states as supervision (Zhang et al., 2025), reconstructing intermediate states from successful trajectories to sample progressive suffix continuations (CRPS, Zhang & Yang, 2026), checkpointing environment and context snapshots for verifier-guided branching (SPROUT, Liu et al., 2026a), and forking rollouts for process credit or distillation (Counterfactual Rollout Replay, Li et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Luo et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Building on restored-state continuation, our study branches from archived frontier mornings against reference economic profit and tests which operational behaviors transfer to an unseen business under fixed instructions. 9 Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences 7.3. Prompt Support and Likelihood-Grounded RL In-context reflection and cross-episode learning methods extract reusable guidance or adapt online across episodes (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2026; Shalev et al., 2026), while Song et al. (2026) analyze posttraining through reward-weighted likelihood over sampled rollouts. Within critic-free group objectives (Kool et al., 2019; Ahmadian et al., 2024), Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) and DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) address length biases on singleturn reasoning tasks, whereas binary reference-profit rewards (MaxRL, Tajwar et al., 2026) remove dependence on episode-failure penalty magnitudes and CISPO (MiniMax et al., 2025) clips the importance weights used in the policy update. 7.4. Operations Research and Supply-Chain Agents Inventory theory characterizes censored demand estimation (Huh & Rusmevichientong, 2009; Besbes & Muharremoglu, 2013; Wang et al., 2025), perishable lot lifetimes (Nahmias, 1982; 2011), and dual sourcing between costly emergency supply and longer-lead wholesale orders (Whittemore & Saunders, 1977; Veeraraghavan & Scheller-Wolf, 2008; Xin & Goldberg, 2018). Relative to stylized inventory gyms and negotiation testbeds (Hubbs et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2026b; Long et al., 2026), SMB Bench couples SQL observability, customer retention, supplier reliability, and working capital in single replayable buying desk. 8. Discussion and Limitations SMB Bench uses the same environment to measure failures to act on delayed consequences, test the consequences of missed actions through replay, and improve the resulting decisions. Behavioral audits and replays distinguish recording diagnosis, consistently acting on it, and improving business profit. We used the environments records to identify operational rules and its archived states to create training experience; on an unseen business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently with fewer severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Persistent purchasing and cash-management failures showed what the agent still needed to coordinate to make those commitments economical. 8.1. Benchmark Limitations Three boundaries govern interpretation of the benchmark results. First, all six businesses instantiate single simulated perishable-wholesale workflow with specified customerattrition and supplier-degradation rules rather than live firm deployments. Second, our 42-to-18 screening protocol deliberately selects delayed mechanisms with measurable profit impact ( 0.25% of baseline revenue in at least four stores) across six synthetic businesses rather than an unweighted sample of routine store events. Third, buyer notebooks and provider-returned reasoning summaries are incomplete records of the causes behind model actions (Appendix A). 8.2. Learning Study Limitations and Future Work Three qualifications bound the learning study. First, validation (Business 5) and test (Business 6) comprise one business each, where 12 test quarters resolve roughly $2,300 at 2 SE; although all four fixed-instruction comparisons across those two businesses had positive point estimates using the same trained checkpoint, the sealed-test profit difference (+$1,489 $1,133) should be read alongside reduced protection reversals and large-loss quarters rather than as standalone < 0.05 single-store margin. Second, leaderboard models used the Benchmark Prompt while our complete Qwen3.8 system used the Evaluation Prompt (not run at initial-prompt baseline on Business 6), so leaderboard rank compares complete systems whereas fixed-instruction pairs isolate the weight update; early SFT and RL comparisons also differed in model size (Qwen3.6-35B for SFT) and training instructions (Training Prompt for RL; details in Appendices and D). Third, researchers extracted the quantitative rules from Businesses 14 records and our recordedoffer audit checks individual local buys without dynamic order replay. Extending trained-reflector and cross-episode learning methods (Lin et al., 2026; Shalev et al., 2026) alongside earlier morning continuations (Days 1259) raises concrete next question, whether an agent can autonomously extract candidate operational rules, test their downstream supply and cash costs, and revise its behavior without human interpretation. Daily Execution Sequence and World Audits Within each 90-day episode, overnight and daytime events execute in fixed deterministic order. At 5 a.m., the buyer receives the daily status dashboard and executes SQL queries, quote inspection, purchase-order placement, shortfall-cover updates, and memory edits until calling advance_day. Before store open, arriving supplier trucks undergo dock inspection and cold/cool/warm room capacity checks; accepted cases enter lot-tracked inventory while late or pre-cancelled cases log status updates and automatic vendor claims where applicable. Across the 16-hour store day, walk-in shoppers draw hourly demand against shelf stock, logging grams_sold and hours_out_of_stock. At evening close, lots crossing markdown_after_days step down walk-in retail price (leaving contracted account prices untouched), expired lots dispose to waste, daily overhead and interest accrue, and 21-day or 7-day supplier invoices settle.
